fields.meta_title: Presentation Evaluation Form With Rubric Scores | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a presentation evaluation form that scores talks against your rubric and sends each presenter the results. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Presentation Evaluation Form That Tallies the Scores
fields.hero_description: Build a presentation evaluation form that totals the rubric, averages peer ratings, and saves each score to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: Scores That Go Somewhere After the Talk
fields.features_subheading: A paper rubric waits in a stack until someone adds it up. As a form, each evaluation is totaled on submit and saved as a row.
fields.feature_1:
Rubric totals worked out on submit

Each criterion gets its own 1 to 5 scale and a line describing what a 5 looks like. The app adds up the criteria the moment the evaluator submits, and nobody totals a sheet by hand.
fields.feature_2:
Questions that change with who is scoring

A teacher sees the full rubric, and a classmate sees two ratings and a comment box. Evaluators pick a role on the first screen, and the form shows only the questions for that role.
fields.feature_3:
Results emailed to each presenter

When scoring closes, the app emails each presenter their total, the score on every criterion, and the comments on their talk. You decide whether evaluator names go with the comments.
fields.feature_4:
Peer ratings averaged per group member

After a group presentation, teammates rate one another's contribution. The app averages the ratings each member receives and alerts the instructor when one drops below your line.
fields.feature_5:
A QR code on the closing slide

Audience members scan the code and rate the talk on a phone, one question per screen. Every rating lands in the session's table, and there is no cap on how many people respond.
fields.feature_6:
Code on GitHub, scores in your database

On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository when a school or company wants the form running on its own servers. The scores themselves stay in a database you own.
fields.why_description: A rubric template hands you the criteria. Emergent builds the scoring behind them and keeps each evaluation in a database you own.

fields.tab_content_1:
By the last bell, Nico has his 17 out of 20

Hedda Larrabee teaches 10th-grade history at Mossbank High School and scores each talk on her tablet while the student is still speaking. Her rubric has 4 criteria worth 5 points each. Nico Albescu's talk on the Erie Canal earns 17 out of 20, and the app emails him the score and her comment before the last bell.
fields.tab_content_2:
Every speaker hears from the room by Monday

The Prairie Soil Health Summit puts a QR code on the last slide of every session. After Delphine Arceneaux's talk on cover crops, 46 attendees rate its content and delivery from 1 to 5 on their phones. The Monday after the summit, the app emails her the session's averages: 4.6 for content and 4.1 for delivery.
fields.tab_content_3:
A peer average under 3 goes to the instructor

Renata Sobczak's marketing students present in groups of 4 and rate their 3 teammates' contribution from 1 to 5. The app averages what each student receives. Cole Pettersen, in the group that pitched a campus coffee cart, averages 2.3, and Renata gets his name and his teammates' comments before grades post.
fields.tab_content_4:
Trainers who differ by 7 points talk it over

Osprey Point Freight ends its new-manager program with a 10-minute capstone talk that two trainers score on their own. Rob Feeney gives Bettina Kroll 22 out of 30, and Asha Venkataraman gives her 15 out of 30. A gap over 5 points holds the score, and the app emails both trainers to agree on one number.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Presentation Evaluation Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to turn your rubric into a presentation evaluation form that scores every talk and emails presenters their results.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the criteria before the questions
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write what a 1 and a 5 look like
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose 4 or 5 things you will judge before you write a single question. Carnegie Mellon's Eberly Center describes a rubric's criteria as the aspects of performance that will be assessed, such as argument, evidence, and clarity. For a spoken talk, add delivery and timing.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Give every criterion a short line for the lowest and the top score. "Delivery: reads every slide aloud" is a 1, and "Delivery: speaks to the room, glances at notes" is a 5. Evaluators who disagree on a number can at least point to the same words.
fields.howto_step_3_des: List every kind of evaluator: the instructor, classmates, the audience, a second trainer. Write down which criteria each one scores. A classmate who saw the talk once can rate delivery fairly, while judging the accuracy of the research belongs with the instructor.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Settle when presenters see their scores. A single grader can send results the same day. When 30 classmates or a conference room rate a talk, wait until the form closes, so the first few ratings do not stand in for the whole room's average.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write the decisions from the first four steps into one prompt. Emergent builds the form from it, along with the email each presenter receives. Change anything afterward by prompting again, such as adding a timing criterion for a 5-minute limit.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Have two people score the same practice talk on their own before the real round. Carnegie Mellon notes that rubrics help to ensure consistency across time and across graders. If their totals still differ by more than 3 points, rewrite the score lines they read differently.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Read the first round of scores
fields.howto_step_7_des: After the first real round, open the scores table and look at each criterion's average. A criterion everyone rates 5 tells presenters nothing. Tighten its top line. A criterion with no comments may need an open question beside it.

faq_plan.q: What is a presentation evaluation form?
faq_plan.a: A presentation evaluation form is the sheet an instructor, a classmate, or an audience member fills in to score a talk. Each criterion, such as organization or delivery, gets a rating, and a comment box records what the score alone cannot say. The ratings and comments then go back to the presenter.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a presentation evaluation form?
faq_plan.a: List the criteria and the scale, decide who scores each talk, then describe all of it in one prompt to Emergent's AI form builder. Emergent builds the form, the table that holds every score, and the totals. Score one practice talk with it before the first real presenter.

faq_plan.q: How many criteria should a class presentation evaluation form have?
faq_plan.a: Use 4 or 5 for a class talk. Pick criteria you can judge during the talk itself, such as research, organization, delivery, or visuals. A rubric with 10 lines has you filling in boxes when you should be watching the talk, and students get a pile of numbers with no clear priority.

faq_plan.q: What should a conference presentation evaluation form ask attendees?
faq_plan.a: Ask for 2 or 3 ratings and one comment, because attendees fill it in on a phone as they leave the room. Rate content and delivery separately. A separate score for each tells the speaker which one to work on. Questions about the venue or the schedule belong on a general event feedback form, out of each speaker's results.

faq_plan.q: How soon after a presentation should the evaluation form go out?
faq_plan.a: Open it the moment the talk ends, while the details are fresh, and close it the same day for a class or within a week for a conference. Put the closing time in your prompt, and Emergent builds the form to stop taking ratings once that time passes.

faq_plan.q: How do I write feedback questions for a presentation evaluation form?
faq_plan.a: Tie each open question to a criterion, such as "Delivery: what is one thing to change next time?" The comment then explains the delivery score. Ask for one strength and one change in place of a blank comments box. Keep it to two open questions, or evaluators start leaving them empty.

faq_plan.q: Should a group presentation evaluation form give one grade or individual grades?
faq_plan.a: Give both: one score for the presentation and a separate score for each member's part. Carnegie Mellon's Eberly Center points out that neither group processes nor individual contribution are necessarily apparent in the final product. At work, score the team's talk here and leave each person's contribution to an employee feedback form.

faq_plan.q: How do I keep a group presentation peer evaluation form honest?
faq_plan.a: Keep each student's ratings private from the teammates being rated, and ask for a reason with any score below 3. Carnegie Mellon's Eberly Center notes that students are not always straightforward when evaluating one another or themselves. Compare each peer average with what you saw in rehearsals before it touches a grade.

faq_plan.q: Can a presentation evaluation form be anonymous?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Leave out the name field, and the form records ratings without saying who gave them. For peer ratings, a middle path works well: the instructor sees who wrote each comment, and the presenter does not. Either way, the ratings live in a database you own, and Emergent builds it with the form.

faq_plan.q: Should presenters rate their own talk on a presentation evaluation form?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if you want to discuss the gap between their view and yours. Have the presenter rate the same criteria on the same scale right after speaking, then show both sets side by side. For knowledge a talk cannot show, such as a quiz on the material, use a separate assessment form.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Presentation Evaluation Form That Tallies the Scores'; hero 'Build a presentation evaluation form that totals the rubric, averages peer ratings, and saves each score to a database you own.' covers scoring, peer ratings and storage, not one feature; how-to description is one sentence with the primary.

intent.evidence: Top 10 is rubric PDFs and template galleries; the page gives criteria and score lines (steps 01-02, FAQ 3, 4, 6), a how-to, four use cases (class, conference, group peer, training) and a Typeform/Jotform/AidaForm table drawn from the top 10.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: 'Each criterion gets its own 1 to 5 scale and a line describing what a 5 looks like', 'Delivery: reads every slide aloud is a 1', 'A gap over 5 points holds the score'.

openers.evidence: Every paragraph opens on a full sentence: 'Hedda Larrabee teaches 10th-grade history...', 'Choose 4 or 5 things you will judge...', 'Have two people score the same practice talk...'.

craft.evidence: Short varied sentences; one ', so' ending in step 4 and repeated 'talk'/'scores'/'rubric' recorded as notes only.

voice.evidence: Concrete, unglamorous detail reads human: 'Strong sources. Slow down on the map.', 'A criterion everyone rates 5 tells presenters nothing. Tighten its top line.'

truth.evidence: All four Carnegie Mellon statements match their quoted spans and keep scope (checked on cmu.edu): criteria 'the aspects of performance (e.g., argument, evidence, clarity) that will be assessed'; 'help to ensure consistency across time and across graders'; 'neither group processes nor individual contribution are necessarily apparent in the final product'; 'students are not always straightforward when evaluating one another or themselves', and FAQ 8 keeps CMU's advice to combine with other evidence ('Compare each peer average with what you saw in rehearsals before it touches a grade'). Emergent sentences map to prompt-build, database-owned, alerts, conversational, no-caps, code-export, free-start. Numbers add up: 5+4+4+4=17; 22-15=7 over 5.

distinct.evidence: Own stories (Mossbank history class, Prairie Soil Health Summit, coffee-cart group pitch, Osprey Point capstone); sibling primaries (feedback form, employee feedback form, assessment form) appear only as FAQ link anchors, never headings.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic builder questions, each answered first ('Use 4 or 5 for a class talk.', 'Give both: one score for the presentation and a separate score for each member's part.'); paa --spec pass 10, reject 0, flag 0; hub link in item 2; moat lines in FAQ 5 and 9.
